blocks.text: In Focus: The MFA Review: Northern Illinois University
©Jessica Labatte, Faculty

Each installment of In Focus: The MFA Review highlights a different MFA program for photographic artists, offering readers a concise overview of its identity, curriculum, faculty, student experience, financial support, and post-graduation outcomes. It also serves as a showcase of the creative work produced by faculty, students, and alumni. Rather than functioning as rankings or endorsements, these features are intended as practical starting points—tools to help prospective students compare programs, identify what matters most to them, and make more informed decisions about their graduate education. While certain details shared in these articles may change over time, my hope is that these program snapshots offer a clear sense of what each represents in the present moment.
Thank you to Amy Fleming for completing this interview and compiling all the images/resources!
Institution name: Northern Illinois University
Degree Title: MFA in Art Studio
Location: Dekalb, IL
Link to Program Page: https://www.niu.edu/art/graduate-programs/ma-mfa-art-design.shtml
Link to Application Page: h ttps://www.niu.edu/art/apply/graduate.shtml#ms-education
Instagram: @niu_school_art_design / @niu_photography
©Jessica Labatte, Faculty
Tell us a little about your program. How would you define its scope and purpose?

The graduate program in art and design is comprehensive, leading to advanced study in fine arts, design and media, art and design education, and art history. Graduate faculty and students have distinguished the program with their many awards, honors and professional accomplishments. The graduate studio faculty, students and alumni continue to influence the arts regionally, nationally and internationally. Their work appears regularly in regional and national juried and invitational shows and is exhibited in leading galleries in Chicago, New York and other urban centers both in this country and abroad. They have also assumed leadership positions in regional, national and international professional organizations.

In the graduate program, faculty expertise is supplemented by visiting artists and scholars and by Graduate Colloquium speakers who are eminent in their disciplines. Students benefit from study at a major university with extensive library resources, cross-cultural programs, a multi-disciplinary atmosphere and frequent performances by guest artists and groups in dance, music and theater. Moreover, the university’s proximity to the Chicago metropolitan area facilitates the use of its libraries, galleries, museums, theaters and other cultural resources. https://www.niu.edu/art/graduate-programs/index.shtml
©Jessica Labatte, Faculty
What would you say makes your program special?
If you have a graduate teaching assistantship, graduate students have the opportunity to teach their own class and really get hands-on experience in the classroom.
©Jessica Labatte, Faculty
What specialized facilities are available for student use (i.e. darkroom, lighting studio, print lab)?
We have a full working darkroom, lighting studio, and digital lab with one large format printer and several small inkjet printers.
©Amy Fleming, Faculty
Is your program strictly photography-focused, or does it encourage/allow interdisciplinary work?
No, students take interdisciplinary classes in addition to photography.
©Amy Fleming, Faculty
Do you specialize in a particular area (i.e. documentary, experimental, environmental work)? And once in the program, is a student able to shift their focus if their creative interests change?
We do not specialize in a particular area; students are encouraged to grow and develop throughout their time at NIU, so if their interests change, we support it.
©Amy Fleming, Faculty
How structured is the curriculum? Are there required courses, or is it more self-directed?
Students must take two professional practice classes and their thesis course, but it is mostly self-directed.
©Amy Fleming, Faculty
Does the program incorporate video work or emerging media such as AI, VR/AR, or 3D/360 imaging?

Students are encouraged to incorporate any medium that they see fit for their work. Several of our photography graduate students have used video in their work. They can work with the Time Arts program if they have specific interests in video.
©Emma Vitallo, Faculty
Does the program offer career development support, such as portfolio reviews, workshop/conference attendance, or networking opportunities?
Yes, in recent years we have had graduate students and faculty attend the SPE conference.
What are key graduation requirements (exhibition, thesis paper, portfolio, etc.)?
The graduation requirements are a thesis exhibition, thesis paper, and comprehensive questions from the student’s committee.
©Emma Vitallo, Faculty
Who are your current faculty members? What are their areas of creative interest?

Jessica Labatte: current director of the School of Art and Design but also teaches photography. Her work explores photographic notions of the visible and invisible, the present and withdrawn as they champion beauty in the everyday as a radical gesture in our contemporary moment.

Amy Fleming: current photography lab/area coordinator. Photography as her main choice of medium, she often turns to her camera as a way to cope. By capturing small moments of time passing through video, and documenting herself and her mundane life in photographic form, Fleming is attempting to navigate her life with mental illness.
©Emma Vitallo, Faculty
Are faculty members primarily full-time or adjunct?
Jessica is full time tenured and Amy is full time adjunct.
How involved are faculty in mentoring students beyond coursework?
Given the size of our program, students and faculty have a close relationship when it comes to mentoring outside of the classroom.
How often do guest artists, curators, or critics visit for lectures and/or critiques?
Lectures and critiques for the entire school of art and design are usually open to any student who wants to attend. These happen often throughout each semester.
©Emma Vitallo, Faculty
How many students are admitted each year, and how many are photography focused? What is the approximate cohort size, and what effect does this have on critiques, collaboration, and networking?

The cohort size depends on the year but has ranged from 1 student to 5. The small size does effect critiques and collaboration and network since there are so few students. However, the smaller the cohort, the more one on one time a student will get from a faculty member. Students are also encouraged to collaborate and form relationships with other graduate students in other areas in the school of art and design.
©Drew Dzurko, MFA 2026
What kind of work are current students creating?

Our current 3rd year photography graduate student, Maria Macko, abstracts recognizable images in her photographic compositions by intermingling organic forms, textured surfaces, and decisive, hard lines. She works with alternative photographic processes.
©Drew Dzurko, MFA 2026
What is the total cost of the program (and duration), and what funding options are available?

The cost ranges from $11,000 to $13,500 each academic year. The program is 3 years long. There are scholarships specific to graduate students and students can apply for a graduate teaching assistantship that helps with tuition and fees.
©Drew Dzurko, MFA 2026
Are there teaching assistantships, and what percentage of tuition do they cover?
Yes, you can find more information here: https://www.niu.edu/grad/funding/assistantships.shtml
Are additional grants/resources available to support student projects?
Yes, you can find more information here: https://www.niu.edu/grad/funding/fellowships.shtml
©Maria Macko, MFA Candidate
What types of careers to alumni pursue, and how does the program support students after graduation?
After graduation, students have gone on to teach at the college level and started their own freelance business.
©Maria Macko, MFA Candidate
How connected is the alumni network, and do graduates stay involved with the program?
Yes the students often form close friendships and relationships and lean on each other for support. The students often stay in touch with faculty and the program as well.
©Maria Macko, MFA Candidate
